sections.title: The Alkali Metals
sections.markdown:
Drop a tiny piece of lithium into a bowl of water and it fizzes politely as
it scoots around the surface. Swap it for a same-sized piece of sodium and
the scooting turns frantic. Swap the sodium for potassium and the hydrogen
that bubbles off actually catches fire. Three metals, one family, one clear
message: these elements behave alike, and they behave *increasingly
violently* as you descend their group. That double observation — same
behaviour, graded intensity — is the entire subject of this chapter. The
elements of Group 1, lithium to caesium plus the ghost at the bottom, are
the **alkali metals**, and they are the first family of the Periodic Table
you will study as a family rather than as individuals.

Every objective of record for this lesson, so you can see the whole
territory before we start:

- understand how the **similarities in the reactions of these elements with
  water** provide evidence for their recognition as a **family of elements**
  (spec 2.1);
- understand how the **differences between the reactions with air and
  water** provide evidence for the **trend in reactivity** down Group 1
  (spec 2.2);
- **use knowledge of trends in Group 1** to **predict the properties of
  other alkali metals** — francium is the exam's favourite target (spec
  2.3);
- **explain the trend in reactivity in terms of electronic configurations**
  (spec 2.4C).

One routing note before you start, because this lesson is different from
the last three you have met. Specifications 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 are
**Paper 1 (1C) and Paper 2 (2C) statements**, shared with Science Double
Award. Specification 2.4C — the deep *explanation* of the reactivity trend —
is **chemistry-only**: Paper 2C only, and Double Award candidates do not
need it. So most of this chapter is core territory, with one marked
Paper-2-only summit near the top.

The lesson runs in five movements. First, the physical profile: a family of
low-density, low-melting, knife-cuttable metals, with a trend running down
the group. Second, storage and handling — why these metals live under oil,
and what the name *alkali* actually records. Third, the family evidence:
the shared electronic configuration and the shared reactions, from water to
air to the white compounds they form. Fourth, the explanation summit: why
the reactivity increases down the group, told in terms of distance and
attraction. Fifth, the payoff: predicting every property of an element
nobody has ever seen.

:::prior-knowledge
Four earlier chapters feed this one. **The Periodic Table** from Chapter 4
(u1:c04) — groups are the vertical columns, and elements in the same group
have the same number of outer-shell electrons. **Atomic structure** from
Chapter 3 (u1:c03) — electronic configurations such as 2,8,1, and the rule
that chemistry happens at the outer shell. **Ionic bonding** from Chapter 7
(u1:c07) — Group 1 atoms lose their single outer electron to form 1+ ions,
and the hydroxide ion carries a 1− charge. **Electrolysis** from Chapter 10
(u1:c10) — you wrote half-equations there; one of them returns at the end
of this chapter to explain *why* these metals react with water at all.
:::

:::exam-hint
The question shapes in this chapter are unusually fixed. You will be asked
to write word or symbol equations for the water reactions; to write
*observations* using the right vocabulary (fizzing, floats, melts into a
ball); to compare two members of the family using comparative phrases; to
state or explain the reactivity trend; and — the classic — to predict a
property of francium, or of a fictional element an examiner invents, by
continuing the group trend. The prediction skill is worth mastering
deliberately: it converts every fact in this chapter into an exam answer
about an element you have never studied.
:::

:::misconception
"A metal is a hard, shiny, heavy thing with a high melting point — so the
alkali metals must just be extra-reactive versions of iron or copper." The
physical profile collapses that stereotype completely: these metals are
**soft enough to cut with a knife**, several of them **float on water**, and
their melting points are so low that sodium melts into a ball from its own
reaction's heat. "Very low for metals" is not a footnote in this family —
it is a headline. Judge Group 1 by its own measured profile, not by the
transition-metal template in your head.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.1–2.4C items across the whole lesson — the
family evidence, the water and air reactions, the trend vocabulary and the
francium-style predictions. If you can already say what all Group 1
electronic configurations have in common — exactly one electron in the
outer shell — the family portrait ahead will assemble itself for you.
:::

sections.title: Storage and Handling
sections.markdown:
Ask a simple question: what does a metal that reacts vigorously with *both*
of the two most common substances on Earth — air and water — need in order
to survive? The answer is isolation. **All the alkali metals are extremely
reactive, and they get more reactive as you go down the group.** They react
quickly with the oxygen in air to form **[[oxide]]**, and they react
rapidly with water to form **strongly [[alkaline]] solutions** of
the metal **[[hydroxide]]**. That second reaction is where the
family's name comes from: an *alkali* is a soluble base, and these metals
literally make alkalis when they meet water. The name **alkali metals** is
a behaviour report, not an accident.

The isolation is real and physical. **Lithium, sodium and potassium are
stored under oil** — you will see them in a school lab as dull lumps
suspended in a jar of colourless liquid. Oil keeps out both the oxygen and
the water vapour of the air, so the metal inside stays as unreacted as the
day it was cut. **Rubidium and caesium are so reactive that oil is not
enough**: they are stored in **sealed glass tubes** to remove any
possibility of oxygen reaching them. The storage regime *is* the reactivity
trend made visible — the harsher the containment, the more violent the
metal.

Handling rules follow the same logic, and they are strict. Great care must
be taken **never to touch these metals with bare fingers**. There could be
enough sweat on your skin — sweat is mostly water, with dissolved salts —
to start a reaction on your hand, producing a lot of heat and a very
corrosive metal hydroxide. The metals are cut, when needed, under oil or
with dry tools, and only lithium, sodium and potassium are ever handled at
all; rubidium and caesium are far too reactive for school demonstration.

One notation convention runs through this whole chapter and the exam
questions built on it, so set it now: **'M' stands for any one of the
alkali metals** (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs), and **'X' stands for any one of the
halogens** (Group 7). Equations written with M are *family equations* —
they are true for every member of the group at once. You will meet them
constantly: MOH for the hydroxides, M₂O for the oxides, MX for the salts
formed with halogens. When an examiner writes "an element M in Group 1…",
they are handing you the whole family and asking you to use its pattern.

:::key-point
The storage hierarchy is an exam answer hiding in a lab observation. Ask
"why are alkali metals stored under oil?" and the marking logic wants: they
react with **oxygen** (and water vapour) in the air; oil keeps air away
from the metal; without it the metal would soon be coated in oxide. For the
top of the group the answer extends: rubidium and caesium are reactive
enough to need **sealed glass tubes**. And the family name itself is a
markable fact: they are called *alkali* metals because their reaction with
water produces **alkaline metal hydroxide solutions**.
:::

:::did-you-know
The family was recognised as a family **before anyone knew electrons
existed**. Chemists grouped these elements together purely on the
similarities in their properties — the same softness, the same low
densities, the same water reactions. When electronic configuration was
finally worked out, the reason for the similarity appeared: all of them
carry exactly one electron in their outer shell. The pattern was visible
decades before its cause was.
:::

:::exam-hint
Two classic one-liners live in this section. "Explain why the metals are
stored under oil" wants: react with **oxygen/water vapour in the air**; oil
**keeps air away**; otherwise an oxide coating forms. "Explain why Group 1
is called the *alkali* metals" wants: reaction with water produces a
**metal hydroxide** which dissolves giving a **strongly alkaline
solution**. And if a question shows rubidium or caesium in sealed tubes,
say the containment is harsher **because reactivity increases down the
group** — the storage hierarchy is trend evidence in disguise.
:::

:::misconception
"The oil is there to lubricate the metal, or to keep it cool." Neither.
The oil is a **chemical barrier**: its only job is to keep **oxygen and
water vapour** away from a metal that reacts with both within moments of
exposure. Leave a lump of sodium in the open air and a dull oxide crust
forms in minutes; under oil the metal stays bright and unreacted for
years. A related error — "the oil reacts with the metal slowly" — is
wrong too: the oil is chemically inert to the metal, which is exactly why
it works.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.1/2.2 items on storage and the family name. If
you can already explain why a jar of sodium sits under oil — air contains
oxygen and water vapour, both of which react with the metal — and why the
name *alkali metals* is really a description of their water reaction, this
movement has done its job.
:::

sections.title: A Family of Elements
sections.markdown:
Why is Group 1 a *family* at all? Two reasons, and the second follows from
the first.

**Reason 1: they all have one electron in their outer shell.** The
**[[electronic-configuration]]** read like a
chant, each member adding one filled shell:

| Element | Symbol | Configuration |
|---|---|---|
| Lithium | Li | 2,1 |
| Sodium | Na | 2,8,1 |
| Potassium | K | 2,8,8,1 |

Rubidium adds one more shell (2,8,8,18,1) and caesium one more again — the
outer shell is always a lone pair-free single electron sitting on top of a
complete kernel. That shared outer-shell count is the structural fact
behind everything else in this chapter.

**Reason 2: they have similar chemical properties — and reason 2 is really
just a consequence of reason 1.** Chemistry happens at the outer shell, so
atoms with identical outer shells react identically. Set the family
reactions side by side and the pattern is total:

- they **all react with water** in the same way, forming a **[[hydroxide]]**
  with the **formula MOH** (LiOH, NaOH, KOH…) and **hydrogen** gas;
- they **react with oxygen** to form an **[[oxide]]** with the
  **formula M₂O** (Na₂O, K₂O…);
- they **react with [[halogen]]** to form salts with the
  **formula MX** (LiCl, KBr, CsI…);
- they **form [[ion]] containing an M⁺ ion** (Na⁺, K⁺…).

In every case the metal atom sheds its single outer electron onto
something else — water, oxygen, a halogen — and every case produces the
same 1+ ion. Even the charges are predictable: the **hydroxide ion carries
a 1− charge**, so M⁺ pairs with OH⁻ one-to-one to give MOH (that is the
ionic-charge bookkeeping from Chapter 7, u1:c07, at work). The family
equations are not approximations; they are the outer-shell fact written in
symbols.

This is the evidence structure the exam wants you to articulate for
spec 2.1: the **similarities in the reactions with water** — same products
(hydroxide + hydrogen), same ionic shape (M⁺ and OH⁻), same equations with
only the metal's letter changing — are what justify treating these six
elements as one family. A family is a claim about *shared behaviour*, and
shared behaviour traces back to the shared outer shell.

:::key-point
Two letters, one grammar. **M = any alkali metal; X = any halogen.** Any
equation or formula written with them is a *family statement*: MOH, M₂O,
MX, M⁺. If you learn the family equations with M and X, you have learned
every member's chemistry simultaneously — and you can write lithium's,
sodium's or potassium's equation on demand just by substituting the
letter.
:::

:::exam-hint
Examiner vocabulary for this section: "family of elements" and "evidence"
are the mark-bearing words. A full-credit answer to "how do the reactions
with water provide evidence that these elements form a family?" names the
**shared products** (metal hydroxide + hydrogen), the **shared formula
pattern** (MOH in every case) and the **graded similarity** (same
behaviour, differing only in speed). Vague answers like "they all react
the same" earn the first mark and stop; the formula MOH is the evidence
the mark scheme is fishing for.
:::

:::misconception
"These elements react the same way because they have similar masses." The
masses are nothing like similar — lithium (7) and caesium (133) differ by
nearly twenty-fold, yet their chemistry is the same pattern at different
speeds. The lever that produces the family resemblance is the **outer
shell**: every member carries exactly **one outer electron**, so every
member loses one electron in every reaction and lands on the same M⁺ ion.
Same outer shell — not similar mass — is the family's cause.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.1 items on the family evidence and spec 2.4C
items on electronic configurations. If you can already write the four
family statements — MOH with water, M₂O with oxygen, MX with halogens, M⁺
always the ion — and trace them all back to the single outer electron,
you are holding the chapter's central idea.
:::

sections.title: Reactions with Water
sections.markdown:
Here is the reaction that defines the family. **All the alkali metals react
in the same way with water, producing a metal [[hydroxide]] and
hydrogen gas.** Written as the family equation, with M standing for any
member of the group:

**2M(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2MOH(aq) + H₂(g)**

Read what the products are telling you. The **MOH(aq)** is the metal
hydroxide dissolved in the water — and a solution of any metal hydroxide
is strongly **[[alkaline]]**, which is why the family carries the
name *alkali metals*. The **H₂(g)** is hydrogen, and it is the visible
star of the show: hydrogen gas bubbling off is what makes the reaction
look alive. The hydroxide is the quiet product — colourless, dissolved —
but it is the one that turns the water into an alkali, and it is the one
the equations must never omit.

The reaction is also **exothermic** — a lot of heat is produced — and that
fact does quiet explanatory work in every observation you are about to
meet in the next section. Melting a ball of sodium into shape and igniting
potassium's hydrogen both run on the reaction's own released heat.

So if the reactions are all the same *kind*, what makes the family
interesting? **The main difference between the reactions is how quickly
they happen.** As you go down the group — lithium, then sodium, then
potassium — the metals become **more reactive** and the reactions occur
**more rapidly**. Lithium fizzes briskly but needs a few patient seconds;
sodium skates around its dish in an urgent hurry; potassium ignites its
own hydrogen on the spot. Same equation, same products, steadily
escalating speed. That escalation is the **trend in reactivity**, and
evidencing it with these water reactions is exactly what specification
2.2 asks you to understand: the *differences* between the reactions —
speed, violence, heat output — provide the evidence for the trend.

Keep the logic of the trend-evidence sharp, because it is a favourite
examination framing. A trend is not demonstrated by one reaction; it is
demonstrated by a *comparison across the family*. Sodium versus lithium:
sodium's reaction is faster. Potassium versus sodium: potassium's is
faster again. The comparison *is* the evidence — the reactions with water
are the standard measuring stick the family gets judged against.

:::key-point
One equation, four facts. **2M(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2MOH(aq) + H₂(g)** tells
you: the products (hydroxide + hydrogen), the solution's character
(strongly alkaline — the source of the family's name), the state symbols
(aqueous hydroxide, gaseous hydrogen), and the observation you should
predict (fizzing — hydrogen coming off). Down the group the *only* thing
that changes is rate: more reactive, more rapid, more violent.
:::

:::exam-hint
Equation marks are strict here. The product with water is the **hydroxide
(MOH)** — writing the oxide (M₂O) loses the product mark, because that is
the *air* reaction. State symbols earn their own marks: **2M(s) +
2H₂O(l) → 2MOH(aq) + H₂(g)** — (aq) on the hydroxide because it dissolves,
(g) on the hydrogen because it bubbles off. If asked for the solution's
character, the word is **alkaline** (or "strongly alkaline") — "soapy" and
"basic" without pH context earn less.
:::

:::misconception
"The hydrogen produced comes from the metal." It cannot — the metal
contains **no hydrogen at all**. Every hydrogen atom in the bubbles comes
**from the water**: the metal's outer electrons reduce water molecules,
releasing H₂ and leaving **OH⁻** behind (which pairs with M⁺ to make the
hydroxide). The metal contributes the electron and the M⁺; the water
contributes the hydrogen. That is why *every* alkali metal gives hydrogen
with water, no matter what the metal is made of.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.1/2.2 items on the water reaction. If you can
already write the family equation for the water reaction unprompted, name
both products, and say which one makes the solution alkaline, you have the
measuring stick for the rest of the chapter.
:::

sections.title: With Sodium
sections.markdown:
The sodium reaction is the family's standard demonstration, and you need to
be able to write it and narrate it. The equation:

**2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g)**

One subtlety in that equation is worth a whole mark of care. Strictly
speaking, most of the time the sodium is reacting it is present as
**[[molten]] sodium**, not solid sodium — the reaction's own heat
has melted it into a ball. It is still correct, and expected, to write
**(s)** in the equation: writing **(l)** for sodium has the potential to
confuse an examiner and is best avoided. Use the state symbol for the
metal as it *started*, not as the reaction temporarily reshaped it.

Now the observations — the list the exam keeps asking for, each with its
physical cause:

- **The sodium floats**, because it is **less dense than water**.
- **It melts into a small ball**, because its melting point is low and the
  reaction produces **a lot of heat** — enough to take the metal past its
  melting point almost instantly.
- **There is fizzing**, because **hydrogen gas** is produced.
- **The sodium moves around on the water's surface**, because the hydrogen
  is not given off symmetrically — the escaping gas pushes the ball in
  random directions like a jet.
- A **white trail** forms behind it: that is the **sodium hydroxide**,
  which dissolves in the water to form a **strongly [[alkaline]]**
  solution (add universal indicator and the water turns purple).

**Lithium** runs the same reaction with the same equation shape —
**2Li(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2LiOH(aq) + H₂(g)** — but **slower**. Lithium's
melting point is higher and the heat is produced more slowly, so the metal
**does not melt**; it simply fizzes and slides around as a solid piece,
taking noticeably longer to disappear.

**Potassium** runs faster than sodium — **2K(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2KOH(aq) +
H₂(g)** — and there is one headline difference: **enough heat is produced
to ignite the hydrogen, which burns with a lilac flame**. The reaction
often ends with the potassium spitting around and exploding. With sodium
the hydrogen usually does *not* light; with potassium it nearly always
does. That flame is the single most examinable sodium-versus-potassium
contrast.

At the very top of the family the reaction leaves the classroom:
**rubidium and caesium react so violently that the reactions are too
hazardous to attempt in school — they would explode.**

:::exam-hint
Observation vocabulary is marked precisely. Write **"fizzing"**,
**"bubbling"** or **"effervescing"** — not "a gas is given off", because
fizzing is what you actually *see* (the gas is an inference). When asked
to **compare** lithium and sodium, use visible-rate phrases: *"fizzes more
slowly"*, *"moves around more slowly"*, *"takes longer to disappear"*.
When comparing **potassium with sodium**: *"fizzes more vigorously"*,
*"moves around more quickly"*, *"disappears more quickly"* — and the key
difference, *"the hydrogen bursts into flames (lilac), which sodium's does
not"*. Comparative sentences, not vibes: each phrase is a mark.
:::

:::safety
The reactions of rubidium and caesium with water would be **too hazardous
to attempt in school** — they would explode. Demonstration work stays with
lithium, sodium and potassium, in very small pieces, behind a screen, with
eye protection: these reactions are energetic and produce strongly
alkaline, corrosive hydroxide solutions.
:::

:::misconception
"The alkali metals react with water because water is hot or acidic." No —
pure, cold, neutral water reacts with every member of the family. The
driver is not the water being hostile; it is the metal's outer electron
being *loseable*. Watch what the electron actually does: the electrons
released by the metal are gained by the **water molecules**, producing
**hydroxide ions** and **hydrogen gas**:

**2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻ → 2OH⁻(aq) + H₂(g)**

You met equations shaped exactly like this in the electrolysis chapter
(u1:c10) — gain of electrons at the cathode. The metal supplies the
electrons; the water receives them. That is the whole reaction, one
electron-transfer at a time.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.1/2.2 items on observations and comparisons, and
spec 2.4C items on the electron-transfer story. If you can already list the
five sodium observations with their causes, and say the one thing potassium
does that sodium does not — ignite its hydrogen with a lilac flame — the
trend in the next section is already half-explained in your head.
:::

sections.title: Explaining the Increase in Reactivity
sections.markdown:
This is the summit of the chapter — and the specification marks it
explicitly: **explain** the trend in reactivity in Group 1 **in terms of
electronic configurations** (spec 2.4C). Understand it as a chain, because
the exam awards the links.

**The fact to explain:** as you go down the group, the metals become more
reactive.

**Step 1 — what the reaction actually is.** In all these reactions the
metal atoms are **losing their outer electron** and forming metal ions.
For sodium going into water:

**Na(s) → Na⁺(aq) + e⁻**

Everything else — the hydroxide forming, the hydrogen bubbling off —
follows from that one loss. So the reactivity question is really a
question about **how easily the outer electron is lost**.

**Step 2 — what makes the electron easy or hard to lose.** That depends on
**how strongly the outer electron is attracted to the nucleus**. The
nucleus is **positive** (it contains the protons), so it attracts the
negative electrons — and the closer an electron sits to that positive
nucleus, the harder it is to pull away.

**Step 3 — follow the atoms down the group.** As you move down Group 1,
the atoms have **more shells of electrons** and therefore **get bigger**: a
sodium atom is bigger than a lithium atom, a potassium atom bigger than a
sodium atom. In the bigger atom, **the outer electron is further from the
nucleus**.

**Step 4 — the conclusion, stated cleanly.** Because the outer electron is
further from the positive nucleus, **the attraction on it is weaker** — so
it is **lost more easily** — so the reaction happens **faster**. Bigger
atom down the group → weaker pull on the outer electron → more reactive
metal. That chain, in that order, *is* the 2.4C answer.

Notice what the explanation is *not*. It is not about mass, and it is not
about eagerness. Potassium is not more reactive than lithium because it is
heavier, and atoms do not *want* anything; reactivity is a geometry-and-charge
story — distance between the outer electron and the nucleus, and the
strength of the electrostatic attraction that distance allows. The
electronic configurations from earlier in this chapter are the map: each
extra shell pushes the outer electron one layer further out.

:::misconception
"Potassium is more reactive than lithium because it is heavier" — the
mass-guess. Mass is not in the chain anywhere; **atom radius is**. A
heavier nucleus with the charge buried under more shells holds its outer
electron *more weakly*, not more strongly. The correct lever is distance:
more shells → bigger atom → outer electron further from the nucleus →
weaker attraction → electron lost more easily → faster reaction. If your
explanation does not mention distance or attraction, it is not the 2.4C
explanation.
:::

:::exam-hint
This whole section is **Paper 2C only** — specification 2.4C is
chemistry-only, so Paper 1 can ask you to *state* the trend but never to
*explain* it this way. The full-credit explanation has four checkpoints:
more shells down the group; atom bigger; outer electron further from the
nucleus; attraction weaker so the electron is lost more easily. Write the
chain as a sentence chain — "the outer electron is further from the
nucleus and so less strongly attracted, so it is lost more easily" — and
the marks follow. (An extension footnote for completeness: reacting with
air can also form **peroxides (M₂O₂)** and **superoxides (MO₂)** — still
M⁺ inside, different oxygen species — and lithium uniquely forms a
**nitride, Li₃N**. Beyond the spec; useful general knowledge, never
compulsory marks.)
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.4C items on the reactivity explanation. If you
can already recite the four-link chain — more shells, bigger atom, outer
electron further out, weaker attraction, lost more easily — and write
Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ to open it, the chemistry-only summit is yours.
:::

sections.title: Reactions of the Alkali Metals with the Air
sections.markdown:
Water is the family's loud reaction; air is its quiet one — and it is the
quiet one you can watch happening on a bench in seconds. **Lithium, sodium
and potassium are all stored in oil because they react with the air**; take
a piece of sodium out of its oil and you can catch the reaction mid-run.

A piece of sodium fresh from the oil usually has a **crust on the outside**
— the residue of its last conversation with the air. It is **not shiny**
unless it has been **freshly cut**. So cut it, and watch:

- the **fresh surface is shiny** — that is what unreacted sodium actually
  looks like, silvery like any metal;
- within seconds the surface **tarnishes rapidly** as the freshly exposed
  sodium reacts with **oxygen in the air**, growing a dull coating of
  **metal [[oxide]]**;
- do the same with **lithium** and the fresh surface **tarnishes more
  slowly**, because lithium reacts more slowly than sodium;
- do the same with **potassium** and the fresh surface **tarnishes
  extremely rapidly** — faster than sodium's.

Read the comparison carefully, because it is a second, independent
measurement of the reactivity trend. **Potassium is more reactive than
sodium, which is more reactive than lithium** — the same ordering the water
reactions gave, now delivered by a *different* reaction on a *different*
timescale. That convergence is what makes the trend evidence rather than
anecdote: specification 2.2 asks you to see the trend in the *differences
between* the reactions with **both** air and water, and this section is the
air half of that evidence.

In each case the chemistry is the same simple story: **metal + oxygen in
the air → metal oxide coating**. No flame is needed for the tarnishing
reaction — oxygen attacks the fresh surface on contact. The oxide layer
is why lab samples look dull and crusted: a piece of "sodium" under oil is
really a shiny metal wearing an oxide overcoat it grew the last time it
met the air.

The tarnishing test is also the fastest qualitative demonstration of the
trend you can perform with no water, no indicator and no flame — just a
knife, three small samples and a stopwatch. Fresh cut, fresh surface, and
the family orders itself in front of you: lithium sluggish, sodium swift,
potassium nearly instant.

:::key-point
Air evidence, compressed: **freshly cut = shiny; a few seconds later =
tarnished** (the oxide coating). Rate of tarnishing ranks the family —
**Li slowest, Na rapid, K fastest** — and it ranks them in *exactly* the
same order as the water reactions. Two different reactions, one trend:
that is the evidence structure the exam wants for the Group 1 reactivity
ordering.
:::

:::exam-hint
The air-reaction marks attach to the *comparison*. "Describe how the
tarnishing of freshly cut lithium, sodium and potassium provides evidence
for the trend" wants: **all freshly cut surfaces are shiny at first**; all
**tarnish** (oxide forms with air/oxygen); and the **rate order** —
lithium slowest, sodium rapid, potassium fastest — showing **reactivity
increases down the group**. Watch your vocabulary: the coating is a
**metal oxide** formed with **oxygen**, and "tarnish" or "goes dull" is
the observable; "rusts" is iron vocabulary and scores nothing here.
:::

:::misconception
"The dull crust on stored sodium means the metal is dirty — wipe it off
and it would be shiny again." Wiping will not help, because the dullness
is **chemically changed metal**: the surface sodium has **reacted with
oxygen** and become a layer of **oxide** — a different substance bonded
onto the metal beneath. Only **cutting** reveals shiny sodium, because
cutting exposes **fresh, unreacted metal** — which then begins tarnishing
again immediately. Dirt sits *on* a surface; this crust *is* a converted
surface.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.2 items on the air reaction. If you can already
say why a freshly cut piece of sodium is shiny but a stored one is crusted
— the surface has reacted with oxygen to form oxide — and rank the three
school metals by tarnishing speed, you hold the air half of the trend
evidence.
:::

sections.title: Compounds of the Alkali Metals
sections.markdown:
The metals themselves are dramatic; their compounds are almost invisible —
and that contrast is itself a family property worth knowing. **All Group 1
metal [[ion]] are colourless.** That single fact settles the colour of
essentially every alkali-metal compound you will ever meet: **their
compounds are colourless or white — unless they are combined with a
coloured negative ion.**

The logic runs one way only, and it is worth getting exactly right. The
metal's own ion contributes **no colour**, ever. So:

- sodium chloride, potassium bromide, lithium sulfate — white or colourless
  solids, colourless in solution. The positive ion is colourless and the
  negative ion (Cl⁻, Br⁻, SO₄²⁻) is colourless too.
- **potassium dichromate(VI) is orange** — not because of potassium, which
  contributes nothing, but because the **dichromate(VI) ion, Cr₂O₇²⁻, is
  orange**;
- **potassium manganate(VII) is purple** — again, not the potassium, but
  the **manganate(VII) ion, MnO₄⁻**.

The diagnostic habit this builds is genuinely useful across the course:
when a Group 1 compound shows *any* colour, the colour belongs to the
**negative ion**, never to the metal. Potassium is a passenger in both of
the famous coloured compounds above; the chromium and the manganese are
doing all the showing.

Beyond colour, the compounds behave as a family too: **Group 1 compounds
are typical ionic solids and are mostly soluble in water.** The strong
ionic bonding (Chapter 7, u1:c07 — positive metal ion to negative ion) is
there in the solid, but put the solid in water and the lattice gives way:
the ions separate and the solid dissolves. That solubility is what made
the water reactions of earlier sections produce *solutions* — the MOH
product does not sit as a solid, it disperses as aqueous ions, which is
why the hydroxide solutions are strongly alkaline throughout.

So the compound portrait completes the family: soft reactive metals that
build white, mostly-soluble, colourless-ion compounds. If an exam question
hands you a white solid that dissolves to give a colourless solution and
asks what the metal ion could be, Group 1 is always on the candidate list —
and if the solid is orange or purple with potassium inside, you now know
exactly which ion is wearing the colour.

:::key-point
Colour assignment rule: **Group 1 ions are colourless; the negative ion
colours the compound.** Potassium dichromate(VI) is orange because of
**dichromate(VI)**; potassium manganate(VII) is purple because of
**manganate(VII)** — the potassium contributes nothing. And the physical
default: Group 1 compounds are **typical ionic solids, mostly soluble in
water**.
:::

:::exam-hint
Colour-prediction questions are free marks once the assignment rule is
firm: **the colour of a Group 1 compound belongs to its negative ion**.
"Explain why potassium dichromate(VI) is orange" wants: potassium ions are
**colourless**; the **dichromate(VI) ion is orange**. If asked for two
properties of Group 1 compounds, the safe pair is "**typical ionic
solids**" and "**mostly soluble in water**" (giving colourless solutions
when all ions are colourless).
:::

:::misconception
"Potassium must be an orange element, because potassium compounds come in
orange." That reverses the colour assignment twice over. First, potassium
the **element** is a silvery metal (with a lilac flame in its water
reaction — a *flame colour*, not a compound colour). Second, in potassium
dichromate(VI) the potassium ion is **colourless**; the orange belongs
entirely to the **dichromate(VI) ion**. Swap the potassium for
colourless-ion sodium and the compound stays orange. The negative ion
wears the colour, always.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.1 items on the family's compound chemistry. If
you can already predict the colour of a Group 1 compound from its negative
ion — colourless unless that anion is coloured — and explain why their
hydroxides give solutions rather than sediments, this movement is done.
:::

sections.title: Summarising the Main Features of the Group 1 Elements
sections.markdown:
Every fact of this chapter now fits on one card. Here is the family
portrait, assembled from the sections above — this list is the exam's
checklist for "state the main features of the Group 1 elements":

- they **are metals**;
- they are **soft**, with **melting points and densities that are very low
  for metals**;
- they have **to be stored out of contact with air or water** (under oil
  for lithium, sodium and potassium; sealed glass tubes for rubidium and
  caesium);
- they **react rapidly with air** to form coatings of the **metal oxide**;
- they **react with water** to produce an **alkaline solution of the metal
  hydroxide** and **hydrogen gas**;
- they **increase in reactivity as you go down the group**;
- they form compounds in which the **metal is a 1+ ion**;
- their compounds are **mainly white or colourless**, dissolving to give
  **colourless solutions**.

Check each line against where you met it. Softness, low melting points and
low densities came from the physical profile; storage from the handling
regime; the oxide coatings from the air reaction; the alkaline hydroxide +
hydrogen from the water reaction; the trend from both — tarnishing rate
and fizzing rate agreeing; the M⁺ ion and the white/colourless compounds
from the ionic chemistry. Nothing on the card is new; the card is the
chapter compressed.

Two lines of that card deserve a second look because exams like to probe
them by contrast. "Very low for metals" is a *comparative* claim — these
metals are soft enough to cut with a knife and light enough to float,
which no everyday metal is, and that is precisely what makes them
remarkable. And "increase in reactivity down the group" is the line that
converts the whole list into a prediction engine: if every property slides
smoothly down the group, then a property you cannot measure can be *read
off* the slide.

Which brings the chapter to its natural question. The summary card
describes five elements you can put on a bench — but the family has a
sixth member, at the very bottom of Group 1, of which **nobody has ever
seen a single piece**. You cannot observe its softness, melt it, cut it
or drop it into water. Does the prediction engine still run? The next —
final — section runs it, and the run is the payoff of everything above.

:::key-point
The one-line family logic, worth memorising as a sentence: **one outer
electron → same reactions (MOH with water, M₂O with oxygen, MX with
halogens) → graded only by speed down the group → so the whole family
portrait is a sliding scale.** Every bullet on the summary card is either
a shared property (from the outer electron) or a slide position (from the
growing atom size).
:::

:::exam-hint
"State the main features of the Group 1 elements" is a list-recall
question — the eight-line card above *is* the mark scheme, and answers
score one mark per correct feature, so write more lines than the marks
available. Two phrasings earn their keep: "**low for metals**" (the
comparative claim — melting points, densities, hardness) rather than
naked numbers; and "**reactivity increases down the group**" stated as a
*direction*, not as a value. If the question adds "explain why they must
be stored under oil", that is the s02 answer — air (oxygen and water
vapour) reacts with the metal, oil keeps both away.
:::

:::misconception
"A summary card means every alkali metal behaves *identically* in every
respect." Read the card again with the trend glasses on: some lines are
**shared properties** (soft, M⁺ ion, white compounds — every member, same
pattern), while others are **slides** (melting point *decreases* down the
group, reactivity *increases*, density *rises irregularly*). The family
agrees on the pattern and disagrees on the speed. An answer that treats
the slide-lines as constants — "they all melt at low temperatures, the
same temperature" — has misread the card.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.1/2.2/2.3 synthesis items on the group summary.
If you can already reproduce the eight-line card from memory and attach
each line to the section that proved it, you are ready to aim the card at
an element no one has ever seen.
:::

sections.title: Predicting the Properties of Francium
sections.markdown:
Meet the family's ghost. **Francium**, at the bottom of Group 1, is
**extremely [[radioactive]]**: one of its [[isotope]]
is produced during the radioactive decay of uranium-235, and it is
extremely short-lived. At any one moment scientists estimate that only
about **20–30 g of francium exist in the whole of the Earth's crust**, and
**nobody has ever seen a piece of it**. There is no jar in any lab on
Earth labelled "francium".

And yet, by the end of this section you will be able to describe it in
detail — because **as you move down a group in the Periodic Table, the
properties of the elements change gradually**, so if you know most of a
group, you can predict the rest. This is specification 2.3 in its purest
form: **use knowledge of trends in Group 1 to predict the properties of
other alkali metals**. The summary card from the last section is the
machine; francium is the demonstration. Take the trend *through* caesium
and the predictions fall out:

- it **is very soft**;
- its **melting point is around room temperature** — careful prediction
  work puts it between **21 °C and 27 °C**, continuing the slide
  (181 → 98 → 63 → 39 → 29 → …);
- its **[[density]] is probably just over 2 g/cm³**, continuing the
  density slide (0.53 → 0.97 → 0.86 → 1.53 → 1.88 → …);
- it **will be a silvery metal — but will tarnish almost instantly** in
  air, because tarnishing rate slides *up* the group;
- it **will react violently with water** to give **francium hydroxide and
  hydrogen** — more violently than any member above it;
- it **will be more reactive than caesium**, the current record-holder;
- its **hydroxide, FrOH, will be a soluble, strongly alkaline
  hydroxide** — the MOH pattern does not break at the bottom of the group.

Study the *method*, because the method is the transferable skill. Each
prediction is a single move: **find the property's slide, place the
unknown at the bottom of it, read off the next value.** The examiner can
run the same trick with a fictional element — call it *edexcelium*, placed
below potassium — and the machinery works identically: its reaction with
water gives an **alkaline** solution (hydroxide + hydrogen, family
pattern); its compound with air has the formula of an **oxide**; its
chloride has the formula **MCl**; its ion carries **1+**. You were never
taught edexcelium. You were taught the slide, and the slide answers for
it.

That is the deepest lesson of Group 1, and the reason this family opens
Unit 2: **a trend is a prediction engine.** Learn the family portrait and
its direction of travel, and you own every member of the group — seen and
unseen alike.

:::summary
One structural fact (a single outer electron), three family equations
(MOH with water, M₂O with oxygen, MX with halogens), two independent
trend measurements (water rate and tarnishing rate, agreeing), one
four-link explanation of the trend (more shells → bigger atom → outer
electron further out → weaker attraction → lost more easily), and one
prediction method (slide + next position) that turns all of it into
answers about elements you have never met.
:::

:::exam-hint
Prediction questions mark the **method**, so show it. For francium — or
the examiner's fictional element — the full-credit pattern is: name the
**trend** ("melting points decrease down the group"), then apply it
("so francium's melting point is below caesium's, near room
temperature"), then land the **family pattern** ("it reacts with water to
give an alkaline hydroxide and hydrogen"). Two-sentence answers that skip
the trend statement score half. And remember the formula patterns
transfer: a Group 1 chloride is always **MCl**, an oxide **M₂O** — the
fictional element's salts are already decided by its group.
:::

:::misconception
"Francium's properties cannot be predicted, because nobody has ever seen
it." That confuses *observing* a property with *knowing* it. The
Periodic Table is a prediction machine precisely because properties
**change gradually down a group** — so the unobserved bottom member sits
at the end of five measured slides and inherits their direction. Every
francium prediction in this section is a disciplined extension of
measurement, not a guess; that is exactly what specification 2.3 means by
"using knowledge of trends".
:::

:::cross-curricular
Francium's story is a physics story too. It exists only as the product of
**radioactive decay** — uranium-235 decays through a chain that passes
through francium — and its most stable isotopes last seconds to minutes
before decaying further. The 20–30 g estimate for the entire crust is a
radioactivity calculation, not a mining survey: it comes from working out
how much francium is being continuously created and how fast it vanishes.
Chemistry fixed francium's place in Group 1; nuclear physics explains why
you will never hold it.
:::

:::can-you
Close the chapter against all four objectives. Can you — (1) **explain why
the water reactions make Group 1 a family**: same products, same MOH
pattern, same ionic shape, differing only in rate? (2) **use the air and
water reactions together as trend evidence**: fizzing rate and tarnishing
rate rank the family identically? (3) **predict properties down the
group**: melting point, density, softness, tarnish speed, water violence,
hydroxide formula — for francium or any fictional Group 1 metal? (4)
**explain the trend in terms of electronic configurations**: more shells,
bigger atom, outer electron further from the nucleus, weaker attraction,
lost more easily (Paper 2C)? If all four are yes, francium holds no
secrets — and neither does any element the examiner invents below it.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.3 items on trend-based prediction — the
francium set and the fictional-element variants. If you can already run
the slide method on an element you have never studied and defend each
prediction from the family pattern, you have converted the entire chapter
into transferable exam power.
:::
